title: Lists
subtitle: The Chalk Wall
martuIntro:
Seven numbers on my wall. I could give each one its own box. I could also lose my mind. A list keeps them together, in order, yes?
You have met lists already. `party.members` was one: the four of you, in order, under one name. Tonight we read a list closely, one position at a time.
goals: Make a [[list]] with square brackets and commas
Read an item by its [[index|position]], counting from 0, and from the end with `-1`
Change an item by its position, grow a list with `.append()`, and join two lists with `+`
Count items with `len()`, and know the last position is `len - 1`
Read a list inside a list, like `roster[3][1]`
Count with `range()`, cut a [[slice]] like `[-3:]`, and sort with `sorted()`

questions.explain: The call hands over 9, so inside the recipe `n` is 9. It works out `9 * 2` and hands back 18. `print` shows what came back.
Python works out the right side first: 18 - 5 is 13. Then `mana` gets 13, in place of the 18.

items.summary: Keep the chalk wall in one list: read it by position, grow it, measure it, and read lists inside lists.

exercises.title: How would you store it?
exercises.martu:
My chalk wall. Hours between bursts, oldest first:
```text
48  48  47  46  44  41  37
```
Store all seven gaps, so you can ask about them later. Any way you like. `hour_1` is done for you.
Try for two minutes, then press Run. There is no wrong try here, yes? If Python stops with a message, that is a try too. Read its last line, then try one box per gap.

anotherWay.label: Seven boxes or one list
anotherWay.text:
```text
seven boxes:
 hour_1  hour_2  ...  hour_7
 [48]    [48]    ...  [37]

one list:
 chalk_wall
 [48, 48, 47, 46, 44, 41, 37]
```

anotherWay.label: Like a shopping list
anotherWay.text: You could write each thing to buy on its own scrap of paper. Or you could write one list, in order, on one page. Same things. One is easier to carry.
Any try is fine. Seven boxes work. Next lesson shows a shorter way.

exercises.title: Make the wall
exercises.martu:
A [[list]] keeps many values under one name, in order. Square brackets hold the list. A comma goes between each two items.
Text in a list keeps its quotes. Numbers need none, so gaps go in bare.
```text
 chalk_wall = [48, 48, 47, ...]
             ^   ^   ^
          bracket  commas
```

anotherWay.label: A shelf of jars
anotherWay.text: Picture a shelf with seven jars in a row. The shelf has one label: `chalk_wall`. Each jar holds one gap. The order on the shelf is the order on the wall.

anotherWay.label: The wall as a list
anotherWay.text:
```text
chalk wall    48 48 47 46 44 41 37
               |  |  |  |  |  |  |
Python      [48,48,47,46,44,41,37]
```
Same numbers, same order. Brackets at the ends, commas in between.
I wrote each gap under the last, oldest at the top. Python reads a list left to right, oldest first. Same idea, turned on its side.
`[`, the gaps with commas between, `]`. No quotes.

predict.explain: `print` shows the whole list: brackets, commas and all. (Text in a list prints with `'` marks, like the Example's `['gold', 'teal']`. Same text, Python's own way of showing it.)

exercises.title: The first is zero
exercises.martu:
Each item has a position, its [[index]]. Positions start at 0, not 1. So `chalk_wall[0]` is the oldest gap. A minus counts from the end: `chalk_wall[-1]` is the newest.
```text
 0  1  2  3  4  5  6
48 48 47 46 44 41 37
-7 -6 -5 -4 -3 -2 -1
```
My check also tries other walls, only inside the check. So read each gap from the list. Never type one you can see.
Seven gaps sit at positions 0 to 6. Try `print(chalk_wall[7])` once and read the last line: an [[IndexError]]. No gap lives at position 7. Then take that line out.

anotherWay.label: Jars numbered from 0
anotherWay.text:
```text
jar:  0   1   2   3   4   5   6
     [48][48][47][46][44][41][37]
```
The first jar's number is 0. Seven jars end at jar 6.

anotherWay.label: Floors that start at 0
anotherWay.text: In some buildings the ground floor is floor 0, and the first floor up is floor 1. Lists count the same way: the first item is at 0.

```text
chalk_wall[0]   -> 48 (oldest)
chalk_wall[1]   -> 48
chalk_wall[6]   -> 37
chalk_wall[7]   -> IndexError
chalk_wall[-1]  -> 37 (newest)
chalk_wall[-2]  -> 41
```
Oogrish counts drills from the first stance, stance 0. Then one, two... He says the first one is only a warm-up. Python agrees with him.

exercises.title: How long is the wall?
exercises.martu:
[[len()|`len(wall)`]] counts the items. The last position is `len(wall) - 1`, because positions start at 0. `len - 1` is always the last position. In Unit 6, loops count from 0 to `len - 1`.
A recipe can take a whole list. Whatever list the call hands over, inside the recipe it is called `wall`. So `newest_mark(chalk_wall)` and `newest_mark([9, 8, 7])` both work.
```text
len(wall)      ->  7
last position  ->  7 - 1 = 6
wall[6]        ->  37
```

anotherWay.text:
```text
position: 0  1  2  3  4  5  6
          48 48 47 46 44 41 37
len = 7 items
last position = 7 - 1 = 6
```

Step 1, on the wall: `len(chalk_wall)` is 7, so `chalk_wall[len(chalk_wall) - 1]` is `chalk_wall[6]`, which is 37.
Step 2, in the recipe, for `newest_mark([9, 8, 7])`:
1. `wall` is `[9, 8, 7]`.
2. `len(wall)` is 3.
3. `len(wall) - 1` is 2.
4. `wall[2]` is 7. The recipe hands back 7.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work?
anotherWay.text: `len` counts from 1, but positions count from 0. So the count is always one past the last position. Take 1 away and you land on the last item, on a wall of any length.

exercises.title: Ranges
exercises.martu:
[[range()|`range(1, 7)`]] counts from 1 up to 7, but stops before 7. The stop number is left out. `list(...)` turns the count into a list you can print.
```text
range(1, 7)
 1 2 3 4 5 6 | 7
             stop: left out
```

anotherWay.label: A ruler
anotherWay.text:
```text
range(1, 9)
|--|--|--|--|--|--|--|--|
1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8  9
^ start          stop ^
```
The stop mark is where you stop. You don't take it.

anotherWay.label: range or randint?
anotherWay.text: `random.randint(1, 8)` rolls ONE face, and 8 can come up. `list(range(1, 9))` lists EVERY face, and the 9 is left out. Different jobs, different ends.

1. Start at 1.
2. Count up by one.
3. Stop before the stop number.
4. `list(...)` collects them.
`range(a, b)`: from `a`, up to but not including `b`.

exercises.title: Slice the wall
exercises.martu:
A [[slice]] copies part of a list. `chalk_wall[2:5]` takes positions 2, 3 and 4. The end is left out, like `range`.
Leave a side empty to run to the edge. `chalk_wall[:3]` is the first three. `chalk_wall[-2:]` is the last two.
```text
 0  1  2  3  4  5  6
48 48 47 46 44 41 37
      [2:5] -> 47 46 44
```

anotherWay.label: Cut marks
anotherWay.text:
Cuts go BETWEEN the items:
```text
 | 48 | 48 | 47 | 46 |
 0    1    2    3    4
```
`[1:3]` cuts at 1 and at 3. What lies between: 48 and 47.

`chalk_wall[-3:]`:
1. Start 3 from the end: position -3, the 44.
2. No end number, so run to the edge.
3. You get `[44, 41, 37]`, a new list.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work?
anotherWay.text: A slice is a new list. Python copies the items out. Change `last_three` later, and `chalk_wall` stays the same. Change the wall, and the copy you made stays the same too.
`[a:b]`: from `a`, stop before `b`. Leave a side empty to reach the edge.

exercises.title: `sorted` or `.sort`
exercises.martu:
Two ways to sort. [[sorted()|`sorted(chalk_wall)`]] hands back a new list, smallest first. The wall stays as it is.
`chalk_wall.sort()` sorts the wall itself and hands back nothing. So `x = chalk_wall.sort()` puts `None` in `x`: nothing came back, like a recipe with no `return`.

anotherWay.label: A copy or the original
anotherWay.text: `sorted()` is a friend who copies your list onto a new page, in order. `.sort()` rearranges your own page and hands you nothing back.

`x = chalk_wall.sort()`:
1. `.sort()` sorts `chalk_wall` itself.
2. It hands back nothing: `None`.
3. `x` gets that `None`.
`x = sorted(chalk_wall)`: `x` gets a new, sorted list.

anotherWay.label: A recipe with no return
anotherWay.text: In Unit 3, a recipe with no `return` handed back `None`. `.sort()` is like that: it does its job and hands back nothing. `sorted()` has a `return`, so to speak.

Not this: `shortest_first = chalk_wall.sort()` (`None`: nothing came back). Not this: `shortest_first = chalk_wall` (the same list, a second name).
This: `shortest_first = sorted(chalk_wall)`.

items.title: Oogrish's Training Log
items.summary: Keep Oogrish's yard log as a list of pairs: add a drill, fix a score, and hand back the newest one.
items.intro:
Oogrish trains in the yard every morning. Cane, shield, breath. He gives each drill a score, and he wants a log.
Each drill is a pair: `[drill, score]`. The log is a list of pairs: a list inside a list.
Six tasks, in order. The comments in the editor mark each one. Any drills you like.
items.martu:
A list inside a list, yes? Outer number first: which drill. Inner number second: `0` for the drill, `1` for its score.
My check tries other logs, with other drills. So read everything from the list, and never type a score you can see.

anotherWay.label: Shelves of small shelves
anotherWay.text:
```text
log[0] -> ["cane parry", 7]
log[1] -> ["shield wall", 5]
log[2] -> ["slow breaths", 9]

log[0][0] -> "cane parry"
log[0][1] -> 7
```
Outer number: which pair. Inner number: which part of it.

anotherWay.label: A score card
anotherWay.text: A score card has one row per drill: the drill's name, then its score. The log is the card. Each pair is a row. `log[0][1]` is row one, the score column.

1. Make the list of pairs.
2. `.append()` one more pair.
3. `log[0][1] = log[0][1] + 2`.
4. The recipe hands back `training[-1][1]`.
5. The drill from `log[-1]`, the score from `last_score(log)`. Glue them, with `str()`.
6. `len(log)`.

exercises.title: Insert and pop
exercises.martu:
Lucky leaned on my wall. A mark rubbed off: the 47.
[[.insert()]] puts an item at a position: position first, then the value. Everything after it moves one place along. No retyping.
[[.pop()]] does the opposite. It takes the last item off and hands it back, so you can keep it in a variable.

anotherWay.label: Squeezing in
anotherWay.text:
```text
before: 48 48 46 44 41 37
place:   0  1  2  3  4  5

.insert(2, 47)
after:  48 48 47 46 44 41 37
```
46 and everything after it moved one place along.

anotherWay.label: A queue
anotherWay.text: Someone cuts into a queue at place 2: everyone behind moves back one. That is `.insert()`. The last person walks off, and you note who it was: that is `.pop()`.

1. `chalk_wall.insert(2, 47)`: 47 goes in at position 2.
2. `newest = chalk_wall.pop()`: the last gap comes off, into `newest`.
3. Print both and look.
`.insert(position, value)` adds. `.pop()` takes the last off and hands it back.

exercises.martu:

items.summary: Eight questions on `range`, `sorted` and `.sort()`, and slices. Retake as often as you like.

questions.explain: `range` starts at the first number and stops *before* the second. So 7 is left out.

questions.q: A d10 has faces 1 to 10. Which `range` makes them?

whyWrong.0: `range` stops before its end number, so `range(1, 10)` stops at 9.
whyWrong.2: This starts at 0, and a d10 has no 0 face. It also stops at 9.

questions.explain: `range(1, 11)` gives 1 up to 10: it stops before 11. `randint(1, 10)` includes both ends instead.
`.sort()` sorts `wall` itself and hands back nothing: `None`. So `x` holds `None`. Like a recipe with no `return`.

questions.q: This should print the gaps shortest first. Mend it.
questions.explain: `sorted(wall)` hands back a sorted copy, so `ordered` holds it. `wall.sort()` hands back `None`.
Position 1 is the second 48. A slice stops *before* its end number, so it takes positions 1 and 2: `[48, 47]`.

questions.q: Fill the blank so the program prints the two newest gaps. Count from the end, so it works for a wall of any length.
questions.explain: `[-2:]` starts two from the end and runs to the very end, so it works for a wall of any length. `[2:]` also prints `[41, 37]` here, but only because this wall has four gaps.

questions.q: Put the lines in order so the program prints the three newest gaps in `wall`, shortest first.
questions.explain: Slice first, then sort a copy with `sorted()`. `.sort()` would hand back `None`, and `[-3:-1]` leaves out the newest gap.
The recipe gets `[9, 8, 7]` as `wall` and hands back `wall[:2]`: from the start, stopping before position 2. That is `[9, 8]`.

items.title: Tuples: Pairs That Stay Put
items.summary: A tuple is a list that can't change: round brackets, read by position, and unpacked into names.
items.body:
Some things come in a fixed shape. A spot on the map of Tor is two numbers: across, then down. A hero's row is a name, then a mana number.
For these, Python has the [[tuple]]. It is like a list, with round brackets instead of square ones:
```python
spot = (12, 5)
```
You read a tuple like a list. `spot[0]` is 12, `spot[-1]` is 5, and `len(spot)` is 2.
But a tuple can't change. `spot[0] = 3` stops Python with a [[TypeError]]: a tuple *does not support item assignment*. And a tuple has no `.append()` at all.
Why want a list you can't change? A tuple says: these belong together, in this order, and they stay put. Nobody changes one by mistake.
Watch your brackets. `[48, 47]` is a list. `(48, 47)` is a tuple. If Python says a tuple *has no attribute 'append'*, you used round brackets where square ones belong.
One more trick, called unpacking. Two names on the left take the items in order:
```python
name, mana = ("Lucky", 26)
```
Now `name` holds `"Lucky"` and `mana` holds 26.

exercises.title: A spot on the map
exercises.martu:
A spot on the map of Tor is two numbers: across, then down. My cabin sits at 12 across, 5 down. The cabin does not move, so a [[tuple]] fits, yes?
Round brackets make a tuple. Two names on the left of `=` unpack it: each name takes one item, in order.

anotherWay.label: Two seats, bolted down
anotherWay.text:
```text
cabin = (12, 5)
         |   |
    across   down
```
A tuple is a row of seats bolted to the floor. You can read who sits where. You can't add a seat.

anotherWay.label: A street address
anotherWay.text: A street address is a house number, then a street. Always both, always in that order, and it doesn't change when you visit. That is a tuple's job.

1. `cabin = (12, 5)`: round brackets, a comma between.
2. `across, down = cabin`: `across` takes item 0, `down` takes item 1.
3. `print(across, down)` shows `12 5`.
`( )` makes a tuple that can't change. `a, b = pair` unpacks it, in order.

items.title: zip(): Two Lists, Side by Side
items.summary: Two lists kept in step, paired up item by item with `zip()`: first with first, second with second.
items.body:
Sometimes two lists go together, item by item:
```python
heroes = ["Oogrish", "Lucky"]
manas = [18, 26]
```
`heroes[0]` goes with `manas[0]`, and `heroes[1]` goes with `manas[1]`. Two lists kept in step like this are [[parallel lists]].
[[zip()]] works like the zipper on a coat. It joins the two sides tooth by tooth: first with first, second with second. Each pair is a [[tuple]].
```python
pairs = list(zip(heroes, manas))
```
Now `pairs` holds `[('Oogrish', 18), ('Lucky', 26)]`.
Why the `list()`? On its own, `zip()` hands back a zipper nobody has pulled yet. Print it, and you see something like `<zip object at 0x7f3a...>`. `list()` pulls the zipper, and you get the pairs.
If one list is shorter, `zip()` stops when it runs out. There is no error. The extra items are left out.
You have seen this. In the campaign, Mar'tu's four replies sat in four boxes, `option_1` to `option_4`, and the game matched `"option 1"` to the first one. Two lists and a `zip()` do that matching.

Every hero's magic has a color. Oogrish's is gold. Gearshift's is fire orange. Two lists, kept in step, yes? The first hero goes with the first color.
[[zip()]] pairs them up for you. Wrap it in `list()`, so you can see the pairs.

items.title: The Basement Inventory
items.summary: Keep the resonance array's parts in two lists that stay in step: insert, pop, sort a copy, count and zip.
items.intro:
Under the trap door, Mar'tu's basement is full of brass. These are the parts of the resonance array, hauled back from the Institute. Bomb Shell keeps the inventory.
Two [[parallel lists|lists kept in step]]: `parts` holds the names, and `counts` holds how many of each. `counts[0]` goes with `parts[0]`. Whatever you do to one list, do to the other.
Seven tasks, in order. The comments in the editor mark each one. Any parts you like.
Before this: the lesson More List Tools (insert and pop), How many times? in Extra practice (`.count()`), and the zip() article.
items.martu:
Two lists, one inventory. If the lists slip out of step, the lens gets the coil's count. Then my array lies to me, yes?
My check tries other lists, with other parts. So read everything from the lists, and never type a number you can see.

anotherWay.label: Two shelves, in step
anotherWay.text:
```text
         0      1      2
parts  lens   fork   coil
counts    3      0      7
```
Position 0 on one shelf goes with position 0 on the other. Insert on one shelf, insert on the other.

anotherWay.label: A shopping list with amounts
anotherWay.text: A list of things to buy, and next to it how many of each. Cross out the eggs, and you must cross out the 12 too. Otherwise the milk gets the eggs' number.

1. `parts = [...]` and `counts = [...]`, same length.
2. `.insert(1, ...)` into both.
3. `borrowed = parts.pop()`, then `counts.pop()`.
4. `sorted(counts)[-3:]`: a copy, so `counts` stays in step.
5. `counts.count(0)`.
6. `list(zip(parts, counts))`.

items.title: One List, Same Answer
items.summary: A stretch: rewrite a seven-box program with one list, so it prints the same thing and works out the shrink itself.
items.martu:
Before you knew lists, my wall lived in seven boxes. The program works. But the shrink is typed by hand, so one new gap and it lies, yes?
Rewrite it with one list. Same three lines, word for word. My check also tries another wall, only inside the check, so read every number from the list.

anotherWay.label: Seven boxes, one list
anotherWay.text:
```text
hour_1 ... hour_7
  48  ...   37

chalk_wall[0] ... [-1]
  48   ...   37
```
`hour_1` becomes `chalk_wall[0]`. `hour_7` becomes `chalk_wall[-1]`, the newest on a wall of any length.

1. Put the seven numbers in `chalk_wall`, oldest first.
2. Delete the seven `hour_` lines.
3. Each print reads from the list: the oldest at `[0]`, the newest at `[-1]`.
4. The shrink is the oldest take away the newest, worked out from those two reads.

campaignLink.why: You have seen this wall. Oogrish ran a finger down it, and the newest number, 37, was circled twice. One list holds the whole wall, so every read and the shrink keep up when a new gap is chalked.

items.takeaway: One list for seven boxes: `[0]` is the oldest, `[-1]` the newest, and the code works out the shrink, so it keeps up with a new wall.
items.pairTalk: Pair talk: before you start, tell your partner which box holds the oldest gap and which holds the newest, and how a list reads each one. Then each of you rewrites it on your own screen.

exercises.title: Make, append, fix, read
exercises.martu:
Lucky copied three marks for you. Make the list, append your guess, mend Lucky's slip by its position, then print the last item, read from the list. My check tries another list, only inside the check, so never type a number you can see.
Stuck? Skip it, or try the lesson Many Values, One Name. Tasks you pass here stay ticked.

items.title: Quick Check 4 · Form A questions
items.summary: Two questions that go with Quick Check 4. To pass the Quick Check, get both right.

questions.q: `chalk_wall` holds `[48, 48, 47, 46, 44, 41, 37]`. `roster` holds four rows: `["Oogrish", 18]`, `["Gearshift", 20]`, `["Bomb Shell", 24]` and `["Lucky", 26]`. What will this print?
questions.explain: `[-2]` is the second from the end: 41. `len` counts the gaps: 7 (the last position is 6). Row 1 is the second row, because rows start at 0, and `[0]` is its name: Gearshift.
`range(1, 4)` counts 1, 2, 3: the stop is left out. `+` joins two lists into one, so the 9 sits at the end as an item of its own, not inside brackets.

items.summary: Three short tasks and two questions, no hints. Pass all three tasks and get both questions right to test out of Unit 4. Stuck on one? The lessons teach all of it, and tasks you pass here stay ticked.

exercises.title: Make, append, fix, read
exercises.martu:
Bomb Shell's Velocite ore powers everything. This list is how many chunks he used each day.
Lucky copied three of the days for you. Make the list, append your guess, mend Lucky's slip by its position, then print the last item, read from the list. My check tries another list, only inside the check, so never type a number you can see.
Stuck? Skip it, or try the lesson Many Values, One Name. Tasks you pass here stay ticked.

anotherWay.text: 1. `ore_used = [4, 5, 7]`. 2. `.append()` adds your guess at the end. 3. Position 1 is the second item: one `=` swaps the 5 out. 4. `[-1]` reads the last item, however long the list is.
Square brackets and commas, `.append()`, a change by position, then `[-1]`.

items.title: Quick Check 4 · Form B questions
items.summary: Two questions that go with Quick Check 4. To pass the Quick Check, get both right.

questions.q: `ore_used` holds `[2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 7]`. `drills` holds four rows: `["cane parry", 7]`, `["shield wall", 5]`, `["slow breaths", 9]` and `["roll and rise", 6]`. What will this print?
questions.explain: `[-2]` is the second from the end: 5. `len` counts the days: 6 (the last position is 5). Row 1 is the second row, because rows start at 0, and `[0]` is its name: shield wall.
`range(2, 5)` counts 2, 3, 4: the stop is left out. `+` joins two lists into one, so the 8 sits at the end as an item of its own, not inside brackets.

items.title: Mar'tu's Chalk Notes: Lists
items.summary: Everything from Unit 4 on one page. Printable.

entries.note: Square brackets around, commas between. Numbers have no quotes. (Lesson: Many Values, One Name)
Positions start at 0. `[1]` is the second item.
Negative positions count from the end. `[-1]` works for a list of any length.
Fix a mark by its position. No retyping the list.
Adds one item to the end of the list itself.
`+` joins two lists into a new one. `wall + 33` is a TypeError: `+` needs a list on both sides.
The last position is `len - 1`, here 2, because positions start at 0.

entries.concept: A recipe that takes a list
entries.note: Use the ingredient `wall`, so it works for any list it is handed. `wall[-1]` is the short way. (Lesson: Many Values, One Name)
Outer number first: which row. Inner number second: which item in it.
The stop is left out. `list()` turns the count into a list. (Lesson: Reading the Wall Closely)
A slice is a new list. The end is left out: `[0:2]` takes 0 and 1. An empty end runs to the edge.
`sorted()` hands back a sorted copy and leaves `wall` alone. `.sort()` sorts `wall` itself and hands back `None`: nothing comes back.
IndexError: list index out of range. Three items sit at positions 0, 1 and 2. For the last item, use `[-1]`, never `[len(wall)]`.

entries.concept: Error: round brackets after a list
entries.note: TypeError: 'list' object is not callable. Read a list with square brackets: `wall[0]`.
SyntaxError: invalid syntax. Perhaps you forgot a comma? Inside a list, items are separated by commas.
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable. `x` holds `None`: nothing came back. Use `sorted(wall)`.
How many items are 48. `len()` counts them all. (Extra practice: Reading the Wall)
`.insert(position, value)` squeezes an item in. `.pop()` takes the last item off and hands it back. (Lesson: More List Tools)
`.remove()` takes a value, not a position. `in` asks: is it there?
The biggest, the smallest, and the total, wherever they sit.
Like a list that can't change. Two names on the left unpack it, in order. (Article: Tuples)
First with first, second with second. Wrap it in `list()` to see the pairs. (Article: zip())
